title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The study used a single hosted model (declared model: gpt-5-mini), a deterministic validator, and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms). We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report every paired episode as safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Importantly, the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics made the primary paired estimand uninformative in this run because the single shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation for every task and no validator‑triggered repairs occurred. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded results, an evidence‑based explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into correct, safe device configurations is a critical NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce human‑readable change plans but may produce semantic ordering or dependency errors that text‑level measures miss. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluations—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and deterministically scored—reveal such semantic failure modes and are increasingly used to assess NetOps agents. Generate–Validate–Repair (GVR) architectures pair LLM generation with deterministic validators and automated repair loops to reduce unsafe applications. Prior work demonstrates GVR promise but leaves open empirical questions about verifier efficacy under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that produce informative paired contrasts. This study reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measures the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The paper contributes: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of a preregistered paired GVR evaluation (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) a precise mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact measured quantities; and (3) a failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and prescriptive, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future experiments.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults rather than only textual fidelity. Recent benchmarks and prototype systems show that combining generation with deterministic validation and iterative repair is a recurring pattern in configuration repair and program repair domains. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions for trustworthy NetOps automation. Work on configuration analysis and verification tools provides engineering precedent for verifier design and incremental checks. Our study differentiates itself by (a) preregistering a single primary paired estimand, (b) using shared_initial_candidate semantics to produce exactly paired LLM generations, (c) executing within an emulation‑grounded testbed with deterministic scoring, and (d) archiving per‑call traces and validator traces to permit exact reconciliation between the preregistered estimand and observed analysis artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. Design and generation semantics: The design was paired under shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused across both arms; the guarded arm could request at most one validator‑triggered repair. Task corpus and sampling: Exactly N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were executed and blocked into topology/vendor clusters with composition: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Model, adapter, and validator: The declared model was gpt-5-mini; the adapter family was a hosted GVR adapter with a deterministic verifier (validator id documented in the archive). The adapter contract implies that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics, a paired difference can only arise if the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applies a repair.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: A deterministic emulator+validator produced a binary final outcome (safe vs unsafe) per episode. Predeclared exclusion rules flagged items where validator PASS conflicted with emulator unsafe outcomes, and infrastructure failures after allowed retries would be excluded from the primary analysis and reported in sensitivity analyses. The preregistered retry policy permitted limited automatic reruns for infrastructure errors; no infra failures requiring exclusion occurred in this run.

Statistical analysis: The primary analysis used a paired binary analysis executor that produced a paired contingency table, a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary planned analyses included repair‑iteration counts and model‑call budgets per arm.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and adherence: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one initial generation per task was produced and reused across arms, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics; the model‑call budget was consumed as planned. Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline successes = 240/240 safe (baseline unsafe_apply = 0) and guarded successes = 240/240 safe (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency is n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode; repair invocation count = 0. Representative archived validator traces record validation states and difficulty labels for tasks but show validator PASS for the shared initial candidate in every episode. Planned sensitivity channels (e.g., treating flagged 'possible false‑safe' items as unsafe) were unused because no flags or infra failures occurred.

Subgroup outcomes: The subgroup slices (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) are degenerate: all subgroups report zero unsafe applies under both arms, yielding identical paired outcomes across blocks.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast depends on whether the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or whether the guarded arm modifies the candidate via repair. In this run the single shared candidates passed the deterministic validator for every task and no repairs were invoked; as a result the guarded pipeline could not produce discordant paired outcomes and the paired estimator is degenerate. This mechanistic explanation is supported by execution accounting (one shared initial generation per task), archived validator traces showing PASS for each shared candidate, and zero repair activity.

Design implications and recommendations: If the research goal is to estimate a causal verifier benefit in paired experiments, shared_initial_candidate semantics constrains detectability: (1) allow independent initial generations per arm so the guarded arm can be exposed to generator variability that the validator could correct; (2) enlarge the permitted repair budget (multiple repair iterations) to study repair search behavior and its contribution to safety; (3) strengthen adversary protocols or introduce adversarial perturbation schedules that increase initial candidate failure incidence; and (4) enhance verifier semantic coverage and include cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator execution to detect false‑safe outcomes. These recommendations follow directly from the archived provider‑call audit, validator traces, and repair logs that together explain why the guarded arm could not alter outcomes in this run.

Threats to validity: Internal validity — the shared_initial_candidate choice is an explicit design constraint that reduces generator variability and therefore reduces the opportunity for the validator to change paired outcomes. Construct validity — the deterministic validator encodes a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain. External validity — the task corpus was synthetic and emulation‑grounded and may not capture all production idiosyncrasies across vendors and operator procedures. Conclusion validity — the observed baseline unsafe rate of zero prevents detection of a verifier benefit under the executed contract; future power computations must account for generator variability and adversary strength to produce informative discordant counts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Because the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics and each shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the guarded pipeline could not create discordant paired outcomes. The artifact archive supports these conclusions and the paper provides concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations (modify generation semantics, increase repair budget, strengthen adversary protocols, and expand verifier coverage) for future experiments intended to produce informative paired contrasts about verifier efficacy.

disclosure_statement: Execution used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) via the registered hosted GVR adapter; the guarded pipeline used a deterministic network verifier (validator id recorded in the archived bundle) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration archive is included with the execution bundle). The initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and the preregistration manifest is included in the archived bundle. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously after the lock. The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused by both arms); under that contract paired divergences could only arise if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Execution artifacts (preregistered manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, task manifests, and analysis artifacts) are archived together with the manuscript bundle to permit machine verification; the manuscript text omits run‑internal file paths and low‑level digests except for the single immutable master prompt SHA required by the track. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulation and corpus scope: tasks employed a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; extrapolation to production multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows is limited.
Single model instance: only the declared hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; results do not imply generality across models, prompt variants, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used a single shared initial generation per task; this reduces generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained adaptive adversaries.

Finite verifier coverage: the deterministic validator encodes a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic faults may remain undetected and planned cross‑checks for validator PASS vs emulator unsafe were unused in this run because no discrepancies occurred.
